stimulus.title: Literary Narrative: The Ledger
stimulus.text:
On the last Saturday in August, my grandfather turned the sign on the door of Okafor Cycle Repair from OPEN to CLOSED for the final time. Then, because he could not help himself, he turned it back. “Someone might have a flat,” he said, as though the whole town had spent forty-one years waiting for this particular afternoon to need him. I was fifteen, and I had come to help him pack, which mostly meant wrapping wrenches in newspaper while he told me where each one had come from.

The shop was narrower than our kitchen at home and smelled of rubber and oil and the peppermints he kept in a coffee can by the register. Inner tubes hung from the ceiling like gray streamers. Along the back wall, under a calendar that had stopped at March of some year before I was born, stood the workbench, its surface so scarred by tools that it looked less like wood than like a map of rivers. I had spent whole summers on the stool beside that bench, handing him spokes and pretending to understand what he meant when he said a wheel was “almost true.”

By three o'clock most of the shelves were empty, and I found the ledger. It was wedged behind the drawer of the register, a green clothbound book with a broken spine, and when I pulled it out a few loose receipts fluttered to the floor. Inside, in my grandfather's slanted capitals, were names, dates, and repairs: NEW CHAIN, TWO TUBES, REBUILT BRAKES. Beside most entries he had written PAID and the date. But beside many others, more than I could count at a glance, there was only a small penciled circle.

“What do the circles mean?” I asked. He was on a ladder, unhooking the last of the inner tubes, and he did not turn around right away. “They mean the bike went home,” he said finally. I told him that every bike went home; that was the point of fixing them. He came down the ladder slowly, one rung at a time, the way he did everything now, and took the book from me. He ran his thumb down a page as if he were reading the names with his hand rather than his eyes.

“This one,” he said, tapping a circle, “was a boy who delivered newspapers. His chain broke on a Monday, and if he could not deliver on Tuesday he would lose the route. This one was a nurse who rode to the hospital at night because the buses stopped running at ten. This one I do not remember at all.” He smiled at that. “Maybe he was just a man with a bicycle and no money that week. That happens to people, too.”

I did the arithmetic in my head, the way my mother had taught me to do at the grocery store, and it came to a lot. Not a fortune, maybe, but enough that I thought of the summer he had sold his car, and of the winter he had kept the shop's heat turned so low that he worked in his coat. I wanted to be angry on his behalf. I wanted to find the newspaper boy, who would be a grown man now, and present him with a bill.

Instead I asked whether he had ever been tempted to collect. My grandfather considered the question with the seriousness he gave to bent wheels. “A bill is a kind of door,” he said. “Some people, when you hand it to them, they walk through it and never come back. I would rather they came back.” He closed the ledger and set it on top of the box marked KEEP, not the one marked RECYCLING, though there was no longer any business for it to record.

Near five o'clock the bell over the door rang. A woman about my mother's age stood in the doorway holding a child's bicycle with a flat front tire, and she looked embarrassed to find the shelves bare. “I heard you were closing,” she said. “I wasn't sure.” My grandfather was already reaching for the one pump we had not packed. I watched him kneel beside the little wheel, and I understood, without anyone explaining it to me, why he had turned the sign back around.

stimulus.title: Literary Narrative: The Ledger
stimulus.text:
On the last Saturday in August, my grandfather turned the sign on the door of Okafor Cycle Repair from OPEN to CLOSED for the final time. Then, because he could not help himself, he turned it back. “Someone might have a flat,” he said, as though the whole town had spent forty-one years waiting for this particular afternoon to need him. I was fifteen, and I had come to help him pack, which mostly meant wrapping wrenches in newspaper while he told me where each one had come from.

The shop was narrower than our kitchen at home and smelled of rubber and oil and the peppermints he kept in a coffee can by the register. Inner tubes hung from the ceiling like gray streamers. Along the back wall, under a calendar that had stopped at March of some year before I was born, stood the workbench, its surface so scarred by tools that it looked less like wood than like a map of rivers. I had spent whole summers on the stool beside that bench, handing him spokes and pretending to understand what he meant when he said a wheel was “almost true.”

By three o'clock most of the shelves were empty, and I found the ledger. It was wedged behind the drawer of the register, a green clothbound book with a broken spine, and when I pulled it out a few loose receipts fluttered to the floor. Inside, in my grandfather's slanted capitals, were names, dates, and repairs: NEW CHAIN, TWO TUBES, REBUILT BRAKES. Beside most entries he had written PAID and the date. But beside many others, more than I could count at a glance, there was only a small penciled circle.

“What do the circles mean?” I asked. He was on a ladder, unhooking the last of the inner tubes, and he did not turn around right away. “They mean the bike went home,” he said finally. I told him that every bike went home; that was the point of fixing them. He came down the ladder slowly, one rung at a time, the way he did everything now, and took the book from me. He ran his thumb down a page as if he were reading the names with his hand rather than his eyes.

“This one,” he said, tapping a circle, “was a boy who delivered newspapers. His chain broke on a Monday, and if he could not deliver on Tuesday he would lose the route. This one was a nurse who rode to the hospital at night because the buses stopped running at ten. This one I do not remember at all.” He smiled at that. “Maybe he was just a man with a bicycle and no money that week. That happens to people, too.”

I did the arithmetic in my head, the way my mother had taught me to do at the grocery store, and it came to a lot. Not a fortune, maybe, but enough that I thought of the summer he had sold his car, and of the winter he had kept the shop's heat turned so low that he worked in his coat. I wanted to be angry on his behalf. I wanted to find the newspaper boy, who would be a grown man now, and present him with a bill.

Instead I asked whether he had ever been tempted to collect. My grandfather considered the question with the seriousness he gave to bent wheels. “A bill is a kind of door,” he said. “Some people, when you hand it to them, they walk through it and never come back. I would rather they came back.” He closed the ledger and set it on top of the box marked KEEP, not the one marked RECYCLING, though there was no longer any business for it to record.

Near five o'clock the bell over the door rang. A woman about my mother's age stood in the doorway holding a child's bicycle with a flat front tire, and she looked embarrassed to find the shelves bare. “I heard you were closing,” she said. “I wasn't sure.” My grandfather was already reaching for the one pump we had not packed. I watched him kneel beside the little wheel, and I understood, without anyone explaining it to me, why he had turned the sign back around.

prompt: In paragraph 6, the narrator's reaction to adding up the unpaid repairs is best described as:

choices.text: confusion about how the ledger was kept
choices.rationale: She understands the ledger well enough to add it up.

choices.text: admiration for the customers' honesty
choices.rationale: She wants to bill a customer, not praise them.

choices.text: indignation on her grandfather's behalf
choices.rationale: Correct. She wants “to be angry on his behalf” and to present a bill.

choices.rationale: The sum “came to a lot,” so she is not relieved.
